title: Session 10 — Waterproofing
text:
What you build today
A potted PCB, a lubricated and sealed gearbox, and a robot that survives a static immersion test.






WarningSilicone cure time gates this session



The PCB potting takes 12–24 hours to cure because of the depth. Plan the session so potting happens first and soldering happens after the cure, or across two sittings.

title: Session 10 — Waterproofing
text:
Before you arrive







Parts
Waterproofing box, Kapton tape, silicone sealant, USB-C cable, CorrosionX, white lithium grease


Tools
Needle, soldering iron


Read
This whole page before starting — the ordering matters

title: Session 10 — Waterproofing
text:
PCB waterproofing
First ensure that the assembled PCB fits within the box before anything else.

Tape the bottom side of the box with Kapton.
Fill the bottom of the box with silicone sealant until it reaches the USB port hole.
Carefully slide the PCB assembly in, with the Seeeduino facing the bottom of the box.
Very important! Insert a USB-C cable into the port. This keeps the sealant from flowing into the port, and the cable is a convenient point to hold the assembly by.
Add sealant along the three free edges to fill any gaps, until the sealant reaches the level of the top side of the PCB. The PCB components and contacts should be left exposed.
Let the silicone cure — because of the depth this takes about 12–24 h.
Solder the wires and contacts.
Solder the voltage regulator.
Seal the top side of the PCB. The best method here is unclear. Tested solutions:

Nail polish
Silicone sealant
422C silicone conformal coating (datasheet)



If you are on a v2.0 board
The method changes slightly. See PCB revisions for the v2.0 procedure, including the SD-card trap-door recovery and antenna potting.

title: Session 10 — Waterproofing
text:
Gearbox
By default the gearbox on the FAAV4 robot is not waterproof at all, and it is normal for it to end up completely filled with water once submerged. Over years of use the gearbox proved largely immune to corrosion — after more than a year of repeated use in water, including in Lake Geneva, one was opened and showed no sign of corrosion.
That is not the whole story, and the exception is the reason for this step:






Figure 1: Gearbox and sun gear after a few dives with motor oil lubrication



Severe corrosion appeared on a newer robot after only 3–4 uses in water. The cause is believed to be improper lubrication after cleaning, combined with the absence of the shaft bearing, which let more water in through the front. Motor oil had been used as a substitute lubricant; its low viscosity is believed to have washed it away quickly, leaving the gears dry. Full investigation in Design notes.






WarningUse the right lubricant



A mix of CorrosionX and white lithium grease. Do not substitute motor oil. Several dives have since been performed with the same gearbox that previously corroded, and it now runs smoothly.


Parts that rust: sun gear, planet gears, ring gear, planet shafts. Parts that do not: screws, motor shaft, washers, body, circlip.

Sealing modifications
A few optional modifications to the FAAV structure and assembly process keep most of the water out.






Gearbox waterproofing, part 1









Gearbox waterproofing, part 2











NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



PCB fully cured and potted with contacts exposed, gearbox lubricated and reassembled with the shaft bearing fitted, connector back-shell sealed, and a static immersion test passed with no ingress.

title: Session 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning

Tools

This page in full — the speed limits below explain most of what you will hit

title: Session 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Task sequence

Mount a small flag on the gearbox output so rotation is visible and countable.
Achieve continuous spinning at low speed.
Achieve position control — the output holds against a hand disturbance.
Tune the loop and characterise your maximum usable speed.







ImportantTo be completed by the instructor

title: Session 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
section: Why low speed is the hard part
text:
Why low speed is the hard part
Regular drone ESCs start losing synchronisation at low speed, which is exactly the regime used for water propulsion. That is the reason this course uses an FOC ESC rather than a hobby unit — see Design notes.

title: Session 4 — Closed-loop control and tuning
text:
Going beyond 600 rad/s
Two issues limit speed: the micro-controller loop rate, and delays from the rotation sensor, which also feed back into the first. The changes below improved maximum speed from 500 to 1700 rad/s, enough to drive the wings at 10 Hz. At very high speeds sensor lag becomes the binding constraint, and shows up as high current draw and noise.

Sensor speed

Switch to an SPI sensor. SPI is faster than I²C or PWM. There is no SPI link directly exposed on the board — the solution is the SPI3 bus, wired as in Session 3.
Increase SPI bus speed to 10 MHz.
Use the AS5047P sensor, rated for speeds up to 28 kRPM.



MCU speed
The goal is to maximise main loop frequency, which reached 13 kHz. Read the current loop frequency with the commander’s F command.







Change
Effect




motor.motion_downsample = 3
+0.8 kHz loop frequency


Disable monitoring
+0.2 kHz


Switch to SVPWM
No improvement observed. May help, unconfirmed


L = 0.0001
Tuning the inductance value helped — made voltage mode work much better





Sensor lag
Compensating sensor lag as speed increases is necessary to go above 500–600 rad/s without wasting current. It is currently hand-tuned every 100 rad/s, and a fitted function is used on the robot. This could be automated by ramping through the speeds and minimising phase current — future work. This SimpleFOC forum thread is useful on the topic.






Figure 1: Optimal sensor offset against speed, for two sensors









Figure 2: Current draw with two different sensors, after compensation









TipAveraging current measurements



When using the ESC’s current measurements (\(I_{DC}\), \(I_d\), \(I_q\), \(I_u\), \(I_v\), \(I_w\)), always average over a time window — the raw measurements are noisy.








NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



Continuous low-speed rotation without loss of synchronisation, position hold against a hand disturbance, and a recorded loop frequency from F.

title: Session 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
What you build today
A brushless motor with a custom shaft pressed into its rotor bell, paired to the Faulhaber gearbox, with the sun gear and the sensor magnet installed.

title: Session 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Before you arrive







Parts
AS2303 KV1500 motor, 4 mm steel rod, Faulhaber 23.04:1 gearbox, M2.5×10 screws


Tools
Circlip pliers, manual arbor press, lathe (booked), cutting oil


Read
This page, and the Motor shaft section below in full before touching the motor

title: Session 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
How the transmission works
The motor is connected via a custom shaft to a gearbox with a 23.04:1 reduction by Faulhaber.1 Both parts are held in place by 3D-printed plates. The output shaft of the gearbox has its own bearing on the inside of the gearbox, and is also supported mid-way on the shaft by a 4×8 mm flanged bearing. This leaves 5 mm of shaft length free for the crank to be mounted on. A flat on the shaft helps lock the rotation of the M3 screw extending through the crank.






Motor shaft







Faulhaber gearbox

title: Session 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Which motor do you have?

Black — AS2303 KV1500 (new)Blue — AT2303 KV1500 (old)



The propeller horn cannot be separated from the bell. You will remove the two screws, then clamp the bell in a lathe using the stock shaft and machine it down (step 4 below).



The horn is a separate part and comes off easily. Skip the lathe operation.

title: Session 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Motor shaft
To pair the motor with the gearbox, the shaft of the brushless motor needs to be replaced. This is a delicate operation — the motor’s structure is mostly aluminium and quite thin, for weight savings.

Remove the circlip on the shaft with the special pliers. Don’t lose it, nor the brass ring.
Separate the rotor from the stator delicately, by hand.
Press the shaft out of the rotor bell.






WarningNever load the bell radially



Press the shaft out very carefully, making sure to never apply forces radially on the bell. Use the manual press with appropriate support below the bell to avoid deforming the dome shape. Do not squeeze the bell with a vice, or even by hand.


Remove the propeller horn, which is not needed — see the tabs above for which case applies to you. On the black motor, machine the bell as follows:






Stock bell







Bring diameter down to 6 mm







Bring the length down to 2.5 mm





Manufacture the new shaft from 4 mm diameter steel rod. It should have a clearance fit through the bearings and a tight fit on the rotor bell. See Figure 1 for exact dimensions.






WarningCheck your wall thickness before cutting



21.5 mm is the shaft length if the motor and the gearbox are separated by a 5.5 mm-thick wall. If your wall is 4 mm thick, reduce the 8.5 mm segment to 7 mm, bringing the total length from 21.5 mm to 20 mm.


Press the new shaft into the bell, making sure not to press on the dome-shaped part of the bell without appropriate support underneath.







Figure 1: Motor shaft dimensions

title: Session 2 — Motor and transmission shaft
text:
Gearbox assembly
The blue part of the gearbox is fixed on one side using the custom screws that come with the gearbox, and with M2.5×10 screws on the other.






ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



Sun gear installation and sensor magnet bonding are in the course project plan but are not documented in the manufacturing guide. Add the magnet part number, bonding agent, and the concentricity tolerance that matters for Session 4.








NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



Shaft seated, rotor spinning freely by hand with no wobble, gearbox mounted, and the sensor magnet concentric with the shaft axis. An off-centre magnet produces sensor faults that are very hard to diagnose two sessions later.

title: FAAV Build Manual
text:
Architecture in one paragraph
One 4S battery (16.8 V max) feeds a custom PCB that steps VBAT down to 5 V to power the flight controller, which in turn generates a 3v3 rail for the sensors on that PCB. Battery power passes through a shunt for current sensing, then out to the ESC. The flight controller commands the ESC over serial. The ESC drives a brushless motor through a 23.04:1 gearbox, and a crank–linkage converts that rotation into wing flapping.

title: FAAV Build Manual
text:
Versioning
This is version fall-2026. Corrections published during the semester are dated in the Changelog. If a step here contradicts what a TA tells you at the bench, the TA is right and this page is stale — report it so the next team does not lose time to it.

title: Design notes
text: Why the robot is built the way it is. Not needed at the bench — useful for your report, and for anyone changing the design.

title: Design notes
text:
Why an FOC ESC
Several ESC solutions were explored for the FAAV concept:

Regular drone ESCs. Hobbyking 12A and EP Aer11 were tested. Both start losing synchronisation at low speed, which is a problem for water propulsion — precisely the regime the robot spends most of its time in.
FOC ESCs tend to be more complex and larger. The G431-ESC1 board is favourable and had already been explored in the lab.

That tradeoff — accepting a larger, more complex driver to get usable low-speed torque control — is the reason Session 3 spends a whole session on the driver.

title: Design notes
text:
Speed ceiling and sensor lag
Maximum speed went from 500 to 1700 rad/s, enough to drive the wings at 10 Hz, through a combination of sensor and MCU changes documented in Session 4. The remaining constraint is sensor lag: above 500–600 rad/s, uncompensated lag shows up as high current draw and noise rather than as a hard speed limit.
Compensation is currently hand-tuned every 100 rad/s with a fitted function used on the robot. Automating this — ramping through the speeds while minimising phase current — is open work.

Open question
Could TorqueControlType::foc_current give better control? The robot currently uses voltage mode, bypassing the current sensors.

title: Design notes
text:
Gearbox corrosion
By default the gearbox on the FAAV4 is not waterproof at all, and it is normal for it to fill completely with water once submerged. This was considered acceptable: over more than a year of repeated use in water, including in Lake Geneva, a gearbox was opened and showed no sign of corrosion.
Then a newer robot, built to experiment with transitions, showed severe corrosion after only 3–4 uses.






Gearbox after a few dives with motor oil lubrication







Sun gear from the same gearbox





The cause is believed to be a combination of improper lubrication after a cleaning event, and the absence of the shaft bearing, which allowed more water in through the front of the gearbox. When an old gearbox was cleaned for installation in the new robot, no proper lubricant was available, so motor oil was used. Its low viscosity is believed to have washed it away quickly, leaving the gears dry and starting corrosion.

Which parts actually rust
Each individual part was left in water for 12 hours.







Rusts
Does not rust




Sun gear, planet gears, ring gear, planet shafts
Screws, motor shaft, washers, body, circlip









After 12 hours in water







Shafts, sun gear and planet gears show rust







Resolution
A few simple optional modifications to the structure and assembly process keep most of the water out. Combined with proper lubrication — a mix of CorrosionX and white lithium grease — this appears to have solved the issue. Several dives have since been performed with the same gearbox that had previously corroded, and it now runs smoothly. The practical procedure is in Session 10.

title: PCB revisions
text:
v2.0 — MIT
The goal of this version was to fix existing functional problems (I²C, pad spacing) and to introduce a new external I²C pad for GPS functionality. It is also designed to function by default with both the newer ESP32S3 chips and NRF52 chips. Improvements in range through WiFi connection are expected. Manufacturing steps are identical to v1.0.

ESP32 compatibility
Hardware and software arrangements were needed for XIAO ESP32S3 compatibility. For software see Software.
Hardware changes: a new PCB housing part allowing SD card removal and reinsertion, a WiFi antenna housing case, and a GPS housing case.
SD card notes

SD cards should be formatted to a specific format (FAT32, believed).
Use non-sharp tweezers to gently extract the SD card from the PCB case — otherwise you risk breaking the card and making it unreadable.
For simultaneous servo and SD card usage, be careful not to use the same pins as on the previous chip for servos; TX and RX are used for SD card communication. You may use the secondary microSD card PCB’s two additional pins.



Waterproofing
The method changes slightly from Session 10. Admittedly it can be vastly improved, but it works:

Insert the assembled PCB, making sure the secondary SD card PCB does not come loose, and that the WiFi antenna is properly inserted.
Insert the USB-C cable into the port, and a microSD card in the relevant slit.
Tape the bottom of the PCB so no silicone escapes when pouring. Pour silicone, using a needle to ensure there are no air bubbles between layers.
When fully cured, the SD card is very hard to remove if the protective section broke off during assembly. It can be salvaged by cutting around three sides of the SD card with a knife and opening it like a trap door, freeing the stuck sections. The trap door can then be sealed with epoxy or more silicone — only on the surface, as you do not want to block the SD card again.

The WiFi antenna should also be potted. Currently the same housing case as for the ESC is used: tape the bottom of the box with Kapton tape, stick the antenna to the bottom of the casing (normally all in sticker form), then pot it with silicone. The silicone layer should be left relatively thin.






NoteThe antenna stops working when wet



It works again once dried. This is expected behaviour, not a fault.




Points for a redesign

Incorrect wiring for pressure sensor — SDA and SCL are swapped.
Cover the vias (currently open vias).
Vias on pads of small SMD components are not optimal for soldering, or just cover the vias.
Increase pad spacing for the cables.
Current sensor: possibly change to a 3.3 V part. Currently a 5 V sensor is used, so current should not exceed \((3.3\,\mathrm{V} - 0.5\,\mathrm{V}) / 0.2\,\mathrm{V/A} = 14\,\mathrm{A}\) without risking damage to the analog ports of the Seeeduino.
UART RX and TX are swapped (resolved)

title: Session 1 — Orientation
text: Week of Sep 9 · Paired lecture: Intro to robotic locomotion · Teams formed today

title: Session 1 — Orientation
text:
What you do today
Form teams, complete shop training, meet the robot you are going to build, and collect your parts kit.

title: Session 1 — Orientation
text:
The robot






Figure 1: The FAAV3.2



The FAAV is a flapping-wing vehicle that operates in air and in water with the same actuation. The build divides into four subsystems, and the sessions follow that order:

Transmission — motor, custom shaft, gearbox, crank and linkage (Sessions 2, 5)
Electronics — ESC, angular sensor, flight controller, custom PCB (Sessions 3, 4, 9)
Aero/hydro surfaces — wings, tail, foam housing (Sessions 6–8)
Waterproofing and testing — potting, immersion, tuning (Sessions 10–12)

title: Session 1 — Orientation
text:
Electronic architecture
One 4S battery (max 16.8 V) connects to a custom PCB that steps VBAT down to 5 V to power the flight controller. The flight controller generates a 3v3 rail for the sensors on the PCB. Battery power passes through a shunt for current sensing on the custom PCB, then back out to power the ESC. The flight controller sends commands to the ESC over serial.

title: Session 1 — Orientation
text:
Before you leave today

Team formed and registered
Shop training complete
Parts kit collected against the parts list
Access to the lab GitHub organisation confirmed







ImportantTo be completed by the instructor



Shop safety requirements, machine access and booking procedure, team size and formation rules, and where the parts crib is. These are institution-specific and are not carried over from the manufacturing guide.








NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



Team registered, kit checked against the parts list, and every member has completed shop training.

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
What you build today
A flashed G431 ESC talking to your laptop over serial, with the angular sensor wired on SPI3 and the motor spinning under commander control.
crumbs: Session 3 --- Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
Before you arrive



Parts
B-G431B-ESC1 board, AS5047P sensor, ST-Link programmer, wire


Tools
Soldering iron, fine tweezers, multimeter


Read
This page, plus Design notes on why we use an FOC ESC









Figure 1: ESC running SimpleFOC, with the ST-Link programmer and the angular sensor
crumbs: Session 3 --- Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
Firmware
Code for the B-G431B-ESC1 motor controller, using the SimpleFOC library, is in the lab repository: FAAV-G431-ESC. See Software for all repositories.
crumbs: Session 3 --- Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
Commanding and monitoring
This is a high-level summary of the SimpleFOC communication docs. Communication with the ESC is over serial, either via the ST-Link programmer (the small attached board) or via a separate microcontroller board.
Once serial is established at 115200 baud, you interact with the ESC through the commander — a practical interface for setting and getting values (instructions). Ask the commander for available commands with ?. Currently available:







Command
Effect




M
Full motor configuration


F
Get the main loop frequency


L
Turn the onboard LED on and off (useful as a comms check)


T
Set the target value — rad, rad/s or N/m depending on control mode


W
Watchdog on/off. If no new target arrives for 1 s, target is set to zero. On by default


R
R0/R1 disable/enable a linear ramp when changing setpoint. RD1000 sets ramp duration to 1000 ms (default 1000 ms). Off by default









WarningCareful when changing control mode



T means something different in each mode — position, velocity, or torque. Sending a velocity setpoint while in torque mode will do something you did not intend, with the wings attached.
crumbs: Session 3 --- Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
ST-Link serial
The ST-Link needs to be connected to the ESC MCU. Out of the box that happens via Serial2, but not once those GPIOs are used as SPI3 for the sensor. In that case you must connect Serial1 to the ST-Link:

Disconnect USART2 and connect USART1: remove R23 and R24 on the daughter board (desolder).
Solder wires to the now-free pins of R23/R24 — the pads closer to U3, further away from the USB port. Connect the wire from R23 to the pad for hall sensor 2 (PB7), and the wire from R24 to the pad for hall sensor 1 (PB6) on J8.
Remap the pins in software for SPI use: in platformio.ini via build_flags, and by overwriting the WEAK PinMaps in pinmap_custom.h. See commit 18520ac on GitHub for details.
crumbs: Session 3 --- Motor driver, sensor and serial

title: Session 3 — Motor driver, sensor and serial
text:
Angular sensor on SPI3
There is no SPI link exposed directly on the board. The solution is to use the SPI3 bus, exposed through a few hardware modifications and matching software changes.



Table 1: SPI3 connections on the G431. * Solder onto the outward side of the resistor.






SCLK
MISO
MOSI
CS




MCU GPIO
PB3
PB4
PB5
PA15


G431B pin
J3
J3
R14*
J3












Figure 2: GPIOs of the G431B-ESC1 board









NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



Commander responds to ? over serial at 115200 baud, L toggles the onboard LED, the sensor returns a plausible angle through a full manual rotation, and the motor spins under a T command.

crumbs: Session 5 --- Frame, crank, linkage and gears

title: Session 5 — Frame, crank, linkage and gears
text:
What you build today
The carbon frame, the CNC-cut crank and linkage, the PEEK gears, and the full mechanical integration that turns motor rotation into flapping. Flapping amplitude is fixed by this design.
crumbs: Session 5 --- Frame, crank, linkage and gears

title: Session 5 — Frame, crank, linkage and gears
text:
Before you arrive



Parts
1.5 mm woven carbon plate, 5 mm aluminium plate, 5 mm PEEK plate, bearings, M2×4 screws, brass inserts


Tools
CNC (booked), drill press, M3 tap, cutting oil, metal glue


Read
This page, plus the CNC guide if you have not run the Stepcraft before
crumbs: Session 5 --- Frame, crank, linkage and gears

title: Session 5 — Frame, crank, linkage and gears
text:
Main body
The main body is a carbon sandwich, spaced 24 mm apart. The plates are CNC-cut from woven 1.5 mm plates, available from swiss-composites; thickness usually varies from 1.5 to 1.6 mm. The top and bottom plates are identical, except for the chamfers needed for the M2 screws. The screws holding plate to plate are M2×4, screwing into brass inserts.






Figure 1: Main carbon frame



Fusion360 generates cutpaths from the parts in the manufacture tab and allows for manufacturing models, where parts can be recombined, realigned and even modified. Here, chamfers were added in the manufacturing model. Operations go: holes first, then chamfers, then pockets, and finally the outline.






Figure 2: Manufacturing model









WarningCheck your zero before you cut



Make sure the machine’s 0 is at the right location in your file, and check the orientation of the axes. Full CNC guide for the Stepcraft D660 is in the CNC reference.
crumbs: Session 5 --- Frame, crank, linkage and gears

title: Session 5 — Frame, crank, linkage and gears
text:
Crank and linkage
Dimensions differ between robot generations — check which one you are building:



Table 1: Crank–linkage dimensions






FAAV3.2
FAAV4




Date
2023
July 2024


Crank radius
4 mm
4.5 mm


Linkage length
23 mm
24 mm


Crank–linkage shaft diameter
3 mm
4 mm


Bearing, crank side
10×3×4
10×4×4


Bearing, wing side
8×3×4
8×3×4 flanged






Both the crank and linkage are CNC-cut in a 5 mm aluminium plate. The linkage is only 4 mm thick, cut down from 5 mm with a facing operation on the CNC. Use a 2 mm endmill. Flooding the part keeps the temperature down and gives good results.
Once cut:

Manually drill a 2.5 mm bore hole into the crank, perpendicular to its 4 mm hole and to the flat raised surface. Drill through the part all the way to the 4 mm hole.
Carefully tap an M3 thread. Use cutting oil and make sure to break off the chips.






WarningThis thread carries high forces



It must be done carefully, keeping the alignment between hole and tap.


Press the bearings into the linkage. They may need to be bonded with metal glue if the press fit is not good enough.
Join the crank and linkage with a short 3 or 4 mm shaft, cut to 9.5 mm. The bearing is kept from coming out with a pointy indent on the shaft end. (To be improved.)







WarningAlignment of the linkage, perpendicular to the shafts, is extremely important



An offset of 1 mm is sufficient to destroy the crank-link in a few flights. To ensure forces are not applied radially, use circular offsets (not shown in the schematics) that fit around the shafts and support proper alignment of the linkage and shafts.


Figure 3 shows how the four shafts for the FAAV3.2 should be manufactured. Nothing exotic, but they need to be accurate.








Transmission, top view







Shaft dimensions






Figure 3: Shafts
crumbs: Session 5 --- Frame, crank, linkage and gears

title: Session 5 — Frame, crank, linkage and gears
text:
Gears
Cut in 5 mm PEEK plastic — a high-performance plastic suited to hard environments and high temperatures. The 5 mm plate comes from RS Components. Cutting underwater again gives good results. Keep the advance speed low enough to cut the teeth cleanly.
The primary gear consists of 2 parts, stacked and screwed together. The 3 mm holes where the carbon is fixed need to be tapped with a sharp M3 tap.






TipKeep the tap normal to the surface



Best done in the drill press, which keeps the tap aligned.


The 3 mm shaft is pressed through the two gears’ centre holes — a mildly tight fit at minimum, otherwise glue the shaft. Same for the linkage shaft (also 3 mm), which should be bonded as well as possible; this one matters more, so use glue in all cases.
Between the gears, a clearance of 0.4 mm (inter-axis spacing of 25.4 mm) ensures proper operation without too much backlash.






Transmission assembled







Transmission, second view











NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



Frame assembled, crank–linkage rotating freely through a full cycle with no binding, linkage visibly perpendicular to the shafts, and gear backlash checked.

Electronic architecture
One 4S (max 16.8 V) battery is connected to a custom PCB that steps VBAT down to 5 V to power the flight controller. The flight controller generates a 3v3 rail to power the sensors on the custom PCB. Battery power goes through a shunt for sensing on the custom PCB, then back out to power the ESC. The flight controller sends commands to the ESC over serial.

title: Session 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Flight controller






Figure 1: Microcontroller in its waterproofing box



Firmware lives in FAAV-Flight-Controller (ESP32, FreeRTOS tasks). See Software for older variants.
crumbs: Session 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

title: Session 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Assembling the PCB
As of April 2026 the current board is v3.0: 4 layers, 21 × 28.5 mm, 34 components. The complete BOM is in the Manufacturing/Assembly folder of the FAAV-PCB-v3 repository.
The simplest way to assemble a FAAV PCB is with a stencil, solder paste applied with a cutter blade, then reflow on the hotplate.






Tape blank PCBs around the PCB to assemble







Align the stencil on top and tape it, making sure it sits flat











Wipe down solder paste with a blade in one firm pass







Place the assembled PCB on the hot plate
crumbs: Session 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

title: Session 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Taking the PCB into operation
Once assembled, solder power wires for VBAT and GND at the input side of the board. Follow these steps before powering the PCB for the first time:

Check that there is no short circuit between GND and 5V / 3.3V / VBAT.
Connect a 15 V supply with a 100 mA current limit to the battery pads and check that it does not draw excessive current.
Check with a multimeter that the buck regulator outputs 5 V from the 15 V input. The MCU should be on by then.

With the MCU powered, flash your test firmware and check the connection to all sensors. Table 1 gives the I²C addresses.



Table 1: I²C addresses





Component
I²C address (bin)
I²C address (hex)




Pressure sensor
0b1110110
0x76


IMU
0b1101000
0x68


INA228 power monitor
0b0101000
0x40






Verify:

Voltage, current and temperature readings from the INA228
IMU readings
Pressure sensor readings
RGB LED control

Once all the hardware on the board is validated, solder the power wires at the output side of the board to the ESC, and the UART wires.






WarningTX to RX



The TX output of the PCB has to be connected to the RX pin of the ESC, and vice versa.
crumbs: Session 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

title: Session 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Connectors
The waterproof connector is the JST 8-pin 08R-JWPF-VSLE-D / 08T-JWPF-VSLE-D. All pins marked _b are used for balancing the battery during recharge. For use on the robot, connect at least Vbat and GND; to allow higher currents, connect Vbat_b and GND_b as well.






WarningSeal the unused cable slots



Do not forget to seal the back of the connector for the unused cable slots — this is a water ingress path straight into the electronics.








Figure 2: Connector wiring scheme. Left: battery connector. Right: connector on the robot / for recharging the battery.
crumbs: Session 9 --- Flight controller, PCB and dry testing

title: Session 9 — Flight controller, PCB and dry testing
text:
Dry testing






ImportantTo be written by the instructor



The dry-test protocol is course material, not in the guide. Needed: what the robot is mounted on while flapping in air, the flap frequency sweep, what is measured, the wireless control setup students reprogram to, and abort criteria.








NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



PCB validated against all four sensor checks, flight controller commanding the ESC over serial, and a supervised flapping run in air.

title: Session 11 — Wet testing
text: Week of Nov 23 · Paired lecture: Fixed-wing flyers

title: Session 11 — Wet testing
text:
What you do today
Immersion, underwater runs, wing trim, and control tuning in water — the regime the whole transmission was designed around.

title: Session 11 — Wet testing
text:
Before you arrive



Bring
Fully waterproofed robot from Session 10, charged 4S pack, spare crank–linkage shaft


Read
This page, and your notes from Session 4

title: Session 11 — Wet testing
text:
Pre-immersion checks

Static immersion test from Session 10 passed, robot opened and inspected dry
Connector back-shell sealed on all unused slots
Gearbox lubricated with CorrosionX and white lithium grease
Watchdog enabled on the ESC (W) — target drops to zero if commands stop
Robot floats level







WarningLow speed is where hobby ESCs fail



Water propulsion runs the motor in exactly the regime where synchronisation is lost. If the drive stutters underwater, stop and check sensor lag compensation before increasing current — see Session 4.








ImportantTo be written by the instructor



The wet-test protocol is course material and has no counterpart in the manufacturing guide. Needed:

Tank or venue, and supervision requirements
Run profile: depth, duration, flap frequency sweep
What is logged, and how it is retrieved — SD card handling on a potted board is not trivial, see PCB revisions
How wing trim is adjusted, and against what reference
Cost of transport measurement procedure, since it is scored in Session 12
Recovery and abort procedure









NoteCheckpoint — TA sign-off



A completed underwater run with logged data, no water ingress on inspection afterwards, and a recorded cost-of-transport measurement.
